blocks.text: A BILL To amend title 28, United States Code, to limit the enforcement of foreign censorship judgments, and for other purposes.
Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled,
SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Guaranteeing Rights Against Novel International Tyranny and Extortion Act" or the "GRANITE Act".
SEC. 2. LIMITATION ON ENFORCEMENT OF FOREIGN CENSORSHIP JUDGMENTS.
(a) In General.--Chapter 181 of title 28, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following:
"Sec. 4106. Limitation on enforcement of foreign censorship judgments

"(a) Limitation On Enforcement.--Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal or State law, a domestic court shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment, or a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state, enforcing a foreign censorship law.

"(b) Right Of Action.--A United States person against whom a foreign judgment described in subsection (a) is entered, or upon whom a judgment, fine, order, or demand described in subsection (a) is served or purportedly served, may bring an action in an appropriate district court of the United States seeking declaratory relief that such judgment, fine, order, or demand is unenforceable under subsection (a).
"(c) Definition.--In this section:
"(1) The term 'foreign censorship law' means any law of a foreign state that--
"(A) (i) has the primary purpose or substantial effect of restricting or penalizing expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association;
"(ii) targets expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association based on its content, viewpoint, or speaker identity; or
"(iii) compels disclosure that would reasonably chill that expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association; and
"(B) would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution if recognized in the United States.
"(2) The term 'foreign state' has the meaning given such term in section 1603.".
(b) No Sovereign Immunity.--Section 1605(a) of title 28, United States Code, is amended--
(1) in paragraph (5), by striking "or" at the end;
(2) in paragraph (6), by striking the period at the end and inserting "; or"; and
(3) by adding at the end the following:
"(7) under section 4106.".
(c) Clerical Amendment.--Chapter 181 of title 28, United States Code, is amended by inserting after the item relating to section 4105 the following:
"4106. Limitation on enforcement of foreign censorship judgments.".

cls.function: The GRANITE Act is an amendatory bill that would add section 4106 to title 28 of the United States Code and add a new exception to the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act.
cls.banner: If enacted, this would bar federal and state courts from enforcing foreign court rulings, fines and orders that punish speech the First Amendment protects. It would also let an American served with one ask a federal court to declare it unenforceable, including in a suit against a foreign government.
cls.checks: All families of checks were run. Because this amendatory bill sits in the courts title, the analysis looks first at its fit with the SPEECH Act in the same chapter, the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act, and the surrounding remedies and definitions.

stated.t: To amend title 28, United States Code, to limit the enforcement of foreign censorship judgments, and for other purposes.

marketed.t: Rep. Rulli told The Times that a foreign judgment over protected speech would be "dead on arrival in our courts."
marketed.l: Free Speech Union, citing The Times

marketed.t: Rep. Rulli wrote that the bill would "defend our digital sovereignty and protect Americans from foreign censorship attempts."
Rep. Rulli said: "The constitution protects our right to speak freely. It does not bend to Brussels or London."

ladder.mechanism: The bill would bar United States courts from enforcing foreign rulings that enforce speech-restricting laws, would let a United States person seek a declaration that such a ruling is unenforceable, and would remove foreign governments' immunity from that suit.
ladder.outcome: The intended outcome is that foreign governments and regulators cannot use United States courts to collect fines or enforce orders over speech the First Amendment protects.
ladder.aim: The ultimate aim is that Americans and United States companies can speak and publish online without having to follow foreign speech rules.

a.q: would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution if recognized in the United States

findings.title: The GRANITE Act does not say whether a "foreign censorship law" is a whole foreign statute or only the provision that a ruling enforced.
findings.plain: The bill blocks rulings that enforce a foreign law that would violate the First Amendment. It does not say how much counts as the law: a whole statute, or only the rule used in the case. A broad foreign statute with one unconstitutional part could be treated either way.
findings.tech: Section 4106(c)(1) defines a foreign censorship law as "any law of a foreign state" with a speech-restricting purpose or effect that "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment ... if recognized in the United States." Section 4106(a) bars rulings "enforcing a foreign censorship law." The text does not say whether "law" means a statute, a provision, or a rule as applied to the speaker. Courts would likely look to the provision the ruling enforced, by analogy to the SPEECH Act, which tests "the defamation law applied in the foreign court's adjudication" under section 4102(a)(1)(A) of title 28. That reading is an inference. A court could instead apply First Amendment overbreadth doctrine, under which, in the words of United States v. Stevens (2010), a law falls if "a substantial number of its applications are unconstitutional, judged in relation to the statute's plainly legitimate sweep". Under that approach, a ruling under an overbroad foreign statute could be refused even where the conduct at issue would be unprotected in the United States. The definition has no carve-outs: clause (A) also reaches foreign privacy and data protection orders, harassment orders, laws on nonconsensual intimate images and intellectual property law, and each depends on the same First Amendment test. The HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, takes the case-specific approach. It bars enforcement unless the court determines that "the conduct for which the foreign judgment order was imposed would not have been protected under the First Amendment". Those are that bill's words.
findings.use: A party resisting a foreign judgment over material that is unprotected in the United States can argue that the foreign statute as a whole is overbroad. A party seeking enforcement can argue that only the provision applied matters and that it is valid.

a.q: Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal or State law

findings.title: Section 4106(a) could block foreign defamation judgments that the SPEECH Act lets United States courts enforce when the defendant would have been liable under United States law.
findings.plain: A 2010 law, the SPEECH Act, lets United States courts enforce a foreign libel ruling in two cases. One is when the foreign law protected speech as much as United States law. The other is when the person would have lost in a United States court anyway. The new section applies over other laws and has no such second route, so it could block rulings the older law allows.
findings.tech: Under section 4102(a)(1) of title 28, a domestic court may enforce a foreign defamation judgment if the party seeking enforcement makes one of two showings. Route (A) is that the foreign defamation law provided at least as much protection as the First Amendment. Route (B) is that the defendant would have been found liable under United States standards "even if the defamation law applied in the foreign court's adjudication did not provide as much protection". A foreign defamation law that fails the First Amendment also meets the GRANITE definition of a foreign censorship law, because it restricts expression and would conflict with the First Amendment. Section 4106(a) applies "Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal or State law" and has no equivalent of route (B). Read together, section 4106(a) appears to bar enforcement in cases where section 4102(a)(1)(B) would allow it. This interaction is inferred from the text, and no source has addressed it. GRANITE also borrows the SPEECH Act's definitions in section 4101, under which a "foreign court" includes an administrative body, so a final decision of a regulator such as Ofcom can be a "foreign judgment".
findings.use: A United States author who would have lost a libel case in a United States court, for example under the actual malice standard, could avoid a foreign judgment that the SPEECH Act would allow to be enforced.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4101 (SPEECH Act definitions)

am.label: Leave defamation to the SPEECH Act
am.instr: Section 4106 of title 28, United States Code, as added by section 2(a), is amended by adding at the end the following: "(d) Relationship to Other Provisions.--This section shall not apply to a foreign judgment for defamation, which shall be governed by sections 4102 through 4105."

ops.after: (2) The term 'foreign state' has the meaning given such term in section 1603.
ops.w: (d) Relationship to Other Provisions.--This section shall not apply to a foreign judgment for defamation, which shall be governed by sections 4102 through 4105.

am.cost: This keeps the SPEECH Act's rules for defamation, including the route for defendants who would have been liable anyway, the burden on the party seeking enforcement, removal and fees. findings.title: The declaratory suit in section 4106(b) may not present an Article III case when the foreign regulator has never tried to enforce its order in the United States.
findings.plain: Federal courts can only decide real, present disputes. A foreign regulator that never tries to collect in the United States will say there is nothing to decide. A court may agree and dismiss the American's suit, even though the bill says the suit is allowed.
findings.tech: Section 4106(b) creates a cause of action, but the Supreme Court said in Spokeo v. Robins (2016) that "It is settled that Congress cannot erase Article III's standing requirements by statutorily granting the right to sue". The Supreme Court ruled in MedImmune v. Genentech (2007) that a declaratory action must show "a substantial controversy, between parties having adverse legal interests, of sufficient immediacy and reality". A foreign regulator that issues orders abroad and never seeks United States enforcement can argue there is no immediate controversy, and that a declaration of unenforceability in the United States redresses nothing, because enforcement happens at home. The court decided Trump Media v. De Moraes by denying emergency relief in February 2025, partly because the dispute over Brazilian directives was not ripe. Service of an order on a United States person, which section 4106(b) treats as enough to sue, may help show a concrete dispute. How courts would weigh it is unsettled.
findings.use: A foreign regulator sued under section 4106(b) can move to dismiss for lack of standing or ripeness before any immunity question arises. A United States person who has only received a notice may lose on that ground.

s.l: Spokeo, Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 (2016)

findings.title: Section 4106(b) lets only a United States person against whom a foreign ruling is entered or on whom it is served sue, excluding speakers affected by orders sent to intermediaries.
findings.plain: The bill lets an American sue only if the foreign ruling names them or was sent to them. Foreign governments often send orders to internet providers, app stores or a company's foreign branch instead. The American whose speech is blocked then has no right to sue under the bill.
findings.tech: Section 4106(b) limits the cause of action to a United States person "against whom a foreign judgment ... is entered, or upon whom a judgment, fine, order, or demand ... is served or purportedly served". Orders directed to a foreign internet service provider, an app store, or a United States company's foreign subsidiary are not served on the United States speaker or the United States parent company. Section 4106(a) still bars U.S. courts from enforcing such orders, but there would rarely be a United States enforcement proceeding, and the affected United States person has no claim.
findings.use: A foreign regulator can direct a blocking order at local internet providers rather than at the United States publisher, and the publisher cannot obtain a declaration under the bill.

a.q: compels disclosure that would reasonably chill that expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association

findings.title: It is unclear whether the GRANITE Act covers fines for ignoring foreign information demands, the kind of fine at issue in the 4chan dispute that prompted the bill.
findings.plain: The UK regulator did not fine 4chan for a post. Much of its case against 4chan was about refusing to answer information demands and file a required risk report. The bill covers laws that force disclosures that discourage speech. The regulator will argue that a fine for ignoring paperwork does not restrict speech at all.
findings.tech: Ofcom's orders to 4chan were, in the words of 4chan's counsel, "information demands under Section 100 of the OSA" seeking a "risk assessment report". Ofcom's confirmation decision of April 21, 2026 found breaches including failure to submit the required risk assessment, inadequate terms of service and inadequate age verification, with penalties totaling 520,000 pounds plus daily fines. Clause (A)(iii) of the definition covers a law that "compels disclosure that would reasonably chill" expression, which may reach such demands. A regulator will argue that a penalty for failing to answer an information request or file a report is a procedural sanction that does not restrict expression under clause (A) at all. The bill does not address procedural or reporting penalties directly.
findings.use: A foreign regulator can frame enforcement as a penalty for failing to provide information or file reports, rather than for speech, and argue the penalty falls outside section 4106.

s.l: Preston Byrne, The Lesson of 4chan v. Ofcom, September 18, 2026

findings.where: Section 4106(c)(1)(B), as applied to age verification duties
findings.title: Because the Supreme Court upheld Texas's age verification law in 2025, foreign age assurance orders may not count as censorship under the GRANITE Act's First Amendment test.
findings.plain: In 2025 the Supreme Court upheld a Texas law requiring some adult websites to check users' ages. The bill only blocks foreign laws that would break the First Amendment. So foreign rules requiring age checks, a major part of the UK law that inspired the bill, may fall outside it.
findings.tech: The Supreme Court decided Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025) by holding "that the correct tier of review was intermediate scrutiny" for Texas's age verification requirement for certain websites with sexually explicit content, and that the law "readily satisfie[d]" it. Clause (B) of the definition asks whether a foreign law "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment". A foreign age assurance requirement comparable to the Texas law would likely not conflict, so orders enforcing it would fall outside section 4106. Ofcom's decision against 4chan included a breach of the Online Safety Act's age verification duty. The bill neither includes nor excludes age verification expressly. How far the Paxton holding extends beyond sexually explicit content is unsettled.
findings.use: A foreign regulator can enforce age assurance duties against United States services and argue that, under Paxton, those duties are not censorship laws under the bill.

s.l: CRS Legal Sidebar on Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton (2025)

a.q: seeking declaratory relief

findings.title: Section 4106(b) of the GRANITE Act gives a United States person a declaration that a foreign speech ruling is unenforceable, and no damages or attorney's fees.
findings.plain: An American who gets a foreign fine or order over protected speech can ask a federal court to declare that United States courts will not enforce it. The bill provides no money damages and no repayment of legal fees. That is a design choice. Competing proposals add money remedies, and each option has costs.
findings.tech: Section 4106(b) authorizes an action "seeking declaratory relief" only. A declaration applies section 4106(a) to a specific foreign measure before anyone seeks enforcement, and gives the U.S. person a binding United States ruling that can be shown to banks, payment processors and hosting providers. The bill has no fee provision. The SPEECH Act's fee rule in section 4105 of title 28 and its removal rule in section 4103 apply only to actions on foreign defamation judgments, so they do not carry over. The HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, provides a declaratory judgment, injunctive relief, reasonable attorney's fees and $25,000 in statutory damages. ITIF proposed damages of $1 million per violation or 10 percent of United States-related revenue. R Street warned that statutory damages can bear no relation to the harm suffered. Any money award would be owed by the foreign state, not the United States, and section 1609 of title 28 makes a foreign state's property in the United States "immune from attachment arrest and execution" except as sections 1610 and 1611 provide.
findings.use: A United States person who wins a GRANITE Act suit still pays its own legal costs, which weighs most on small publishers. Adding damages would raise the stakes for foreign governments but would produce judgments that are hard to collect.

a.q: "(7) under section 4106."

findings.title: The GRANITE Act's immunity exception reads only "under section 4106", and leaves slow service on foreign states, comity and act of state arguments, and a narrow reading in place.
findings.plain: The bill removes foreign governments' protection from being sued in these cases with one short phrase. It does nothing about the slow formal process for serving papers on a foreign government. Foreign governments can still raise other defenses, and a federal judge has said this protection exists partly so other countries treat America the same way.
findings.tech: Section 2(b) adds 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(7), "under section 4106." It removes immunity and nothing else. Service on a foreign state must follow 28 U.S.C. 1608, ending if necessary with transmission by the Secretary of State "through diplomatic channels", and the state then has 60 days to answer. The exception does not address the act of state doctrine or comity-based abstention. In dismissing 4chan's suit, the court described foreign sovereign immunity as granted "as a matter of grace and comity" and "motivated in part by a desire for reciprocity". Defendants can cite that reasoning to argue for a narrow reading of the new exception, and it identifies the reciprocity risk Congress weighs when removing immunity. The immunity of individual foreign officials, which the FSIA does not govern, is also untouched, though that matters little when the only remedy is a declaration against the state.
findings.use: A foreign government sued under section 4106(b) can delay the case through the service rules, then argue comity or act of state, and ask the court to read the exception narrowly in light of reciprocity.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 1608 (service on a foreign state)

a.q: a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state

findings.title: The GRANITE Act does not define "demand" and does not reach executive branch cooperation, extradition, or court help gathering evidence for foreign speech cases.
findings.plain: The bill does not say what counts as a foreign "demand", such as an emailed request or a voluntary code. It only stops courts from enforcing foreign rulings. United States agencies can still cooperate with foreign speech cases, and United States courts can still help foreign courts gather evidence.
findings.tech: Section 4106(a) reaches "a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state". The bill does not define "demand", so it is unclear whether an emailed request, a voluntary code of conduct, or a notice from a government-recognized flagging organization counts. The bar applies only to a court that would "recognize or enforce" a foreign measure. A federal court acting under section 1782 of title 28, which allows a district court to order testimony or documents "for use in a proceeding in a foreign or international tribunal", is arguably not recognizing or enforcing anything. Executive branch cooperation under mutual legal assistance treaties and extradition decisions are not addressed. The drafter of the original GRANITE concept says those protections are not explicit in House bill 10174. Wyoming's bill barred state agencies and employees from "cooperating with foreign censorship orders or extradition requests based on speech-related offenses", and the HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, bars officials from assisting foreign enforcement and bars extradition for protected conduct.
findings.use: A foreign prosecutor in a speech case can obtain evidence about a U.S. user through a section 1782 application or a treaty request, neither of which the bill clearly reaches.

a.q: a domestic court shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment

findings.title: United States courts already refuse to enforce foreign government fines, so the GRANITE Act's main legal changes are the immunity exception and a written bar on private parties' judgments.
findings.plain: United States courts have long refused to collect fines for foreign governments. So the bill's ban on enforcing foreign speech fines mostly writes down an old rule. Its new effects are letting Americans sue foreign governments over these orders, and blocking foreign court awards that private people win under speech laws.
findings.tech: The Supreme Court stated in Huntington v. Attrill (1892) that "The courts of no country execute the penal laws of another." That is the rule against enforcing foreign penal laws. State statutes based on the uniform foreign-money-judgments act exclude any judgment that is "A fine or other penalty." The statutes use that wording. In dismissing 4chan's suit against Ofcom, the federal court in Washington observed that "American courts generally decline to enforce foreign judgments that violate the United States Constitution" and "are not necessarily required to enforce foreign penal judgments." Those were the court's words. Ofcom's chief executive told members of Parliament that only two of eleven Online Safety Act fines had been paid, and a report of the same evidence states that four sites had geo-blocked the United Kingdom. In February 2025, a federal court in Florida denied Rumble and Trump Media an emergency order against a Brazilian justice's directives. It found that the directives had not been served under the Hague Convention or the U.S.-Brazil mutual legal assistance treaty and so imposed no obligation to comply. Against that background, the bill's new legal elements are the FSIA exception in section 2(b), which lets a United States person sue a foreign state for a declaration, and a statutory bar on private parties' foreign judgments under non-defamation speech laws. Courts now assess those judgments under the public policy ground in state recognition statutes. That ground allows a court to refuse a judgment "repugnant to the public policy of this State or the United States." For defamation judgments, which the SPEECH Act already covers, section 4106 changes the result in the way described in finding R2.
findings.use: Supporters can describe the bill as stopping foreign governments from collecting speech fines in United States courts, which United States courts already refuse to do. The practical changes are access to United States courts against foreign governments and a firmer, uniform bar against private parties' foreign judgments under speech laws.

findings.title: Whether European Union law and the European Commission count as a "foreign state" under the GRANITE Act is supported by one appeals court but not settled nationally.
findings.plain: The bill uses the federal meaning of "foreign state". One federal appeals court has held that the European Community counts as an agency of foreign states under that meaning. Other courts have not ruled, so the European Commission could still argue it is outside the bill.
findings.tech: Section 4106(c)(2) adopts the definition in 28 U.S.C. 1603, which includes an agency or instrumentality of a foreign state. The Second Circuit decided European Community v. RJR Nabisco (2014) by holding that "the European Community is an organ of a foreign state, and thus an agency or instrumentality", and rejected the argument that an entity serving several states is excluded. The Fifth Circuit has treated entities owned jointly by several states as covered. ITIF states that the International Organizations Immunities Act also protects bodies like the European Commission and recommends reforming it. Wyoming's bill expressly covered international organizations. The Commission's first Digital Services Act fine, 120 million euros against X on December 5, 2025, was for breaches of transparency obligations, such as misleading verification marks and barriers to researcher data access, which may not meet clause (A) of the definition in any event.
findings.use: The European Commission can argue in a circuit other than the Second that it is not a "foreign state" under section 1603, and can argue that transparency penalties do not restrict expression.

a.q: enforcing a foreign censorship law

findings.title: Section 4106 does not say which party must show that a foreign law is a "foreign censorship law", which matters mainly for private parties' foreign money judgments.
findings.plain: Someone has to show that the foreign law punishes protected speech. The bill does not say who. Judges decide most of that as a legal question, so the gap matters less than it seems. It matters most when a private person tries to collect a foreign court award.
findings.tech: Whether a foreign law restricts expression and whether it conflicts with the First Amendment are largely questions of law. Under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 44.1, a court determining foreign law "may consider any relevant material or source", and its determination "must be treated as a ruling on a question of law." Foreign government fines are already outside United States enforcement (finding R10). The allocation matters most for money judgments won by private parties under foreign speech laws. State statutes based on the uniform foreign-money-judgments act provide that "A party resisting recognition of a foreign-country judgment has the burden of establishing" a ground for nonrecognition, so the United States defendant would likely carry it. The SPEECH Act reverses that rule for defamation in section 4102(a)(2) of title 28. The application of the state rule to section 4106 is inferred. The HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, places that burden on the party seeking recognition or enforcement.
findings.use: A United States person facing a private party's foreign judgment under a foreign speech law would likely carry the burden of showing that the law is a "foreign censorship law", the reverse of the SPEECH Act rule for defamation.

a.q: A United States person

findings.title: The GRANITE Act borrows the SPEECH Act's definition of "United States person", whose clause for lawfully resident noncitizens refers only to "the foreign defamation action".
findings.plain: The bill borrows a definition from the 2010 libel law. One part of it covers noncitizens living here legally, but only by reference to a libel case. It is unclear whether visa holders sued abroad under other speech laws can use the bill.
findings.tech: Section 4106 uses "United States person", which section 4101(6) of title 28 defines for chapter 181. Clause (C) covers "an alien lawfully residing in the United States at the time that the speech that is the subject of the foreign defamation action was researched, prepared, or disseminated". For a non-defamation foreign censorship law there is no "foreign defamation action", so it is unclear whether a lawfully resident noncitizen who is not a permanent resident is covered. Citizens, permanent residents and U.S. businesses are covered by clauses (A), (B) and (D).
findings.use: A foreign regulator sued by a United States-resident visa holder over a non-defamation order can argue the plaintiff is not a "United States person" under section 4101(6)(C).

a.q: restricting or penalizing expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association

findings.title: Because the Supreme Court treats platforms' content moderation as protected expression, the GRANITE Act may cover foreign rules on how platforms moderate, not only rules on users' speech.
findings.plain: The Supreme Court has held that a platform's choices about which posts to show, and in what order, are the platform's own expression. A foreign rule directing how a platform moderates could therefore count as a speech law under the bill. The bill could then shield large platforms from foreign platform regulation generally, not only individual speakers.
findings.tech: Section 4106(c)(1)(A) reaches laws that restrict or penalize "expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association", without defining those terms. The Supreme Court has held, in Moody v. NetChoice (2024), that when platforms use their content standards to decide which third-party posts to display and how to order them, "they are making expressive choices". The Court added that "a State may not interfere with private actors' speech to advance its own vision of ideological balance". Under that holding, a foreign law that requires a platform to assess risks, remove categories of content or change its ranking systems arguably restricts the platform's own expression. If imposed in the United States, such a law could conflict with the First Amendment under clause (B). The bill would then reach foreign regulation of platform design and moderation generally. Whether courts would carry the reasoning of Moody over to foreign duties of this kind is untested, so this reading is an inference.
findings.use: A large platform facing a foreign duty to assess or reduce risks on its service can argue that the duty restricts its own editorial expression and that the foreign law is a "foreign censorship law".

s.l: Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 603 U.S. 707 (2024)

a.q: Right Of Action

findings.title: Section 4106(b) names no defendant and has no service rule, so a suit against a private foreign party that won a foreign judgment may fail for lack of jurisdiction.
findings.plain: The bill lets a United States person sue but does not say whom. The opposing party is often a private person or company abroad that won a ruling there. The SPEECH Act allows service anywhere in the United States for its declaratory suits, and section 4106 does not, so a court may lack jurisdiction over that foreign party.
findings.tech: Section 4106(b) authorizes "an action in an appropriate district court of the United States" without naming the defendant. The FSIA exception in section 2(b) implies a foreign state, but many judgments under foreign speech laws are won by private parties. The SPEECH Act has a service rule for declaratory actions under section 4104 of title 28. It provides that "process may be served in the judicial district where the case is brought or any other judicial district of the United States where the defendant may be found, resides, has an agent, or transacts business". Section 4106 has no equivalent. A foreign private party that obtained a judgment abroad and has taken no step in the United States may not be subject to personal jurisdiction in a United States court. That consequence is inferred from the absence of a service rule.
findings.use: A foreign private party that won a speech judgment abroad can resist a United States declaratory suit by contesting service and personal jurisdiction, leaving the United States person without a declaration until enforcement is attempted.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4104 (declaratory judgments)

am.label: Add a service rule like the SPEECH Act
am.instr: Section 4106(b) of title 28, United States Code, as added by section 2(a), is amended by adding at the end the following: "In an action under this subsection, process may be served in the judicial district where the case is brought or any other judicial district of the United States where the defendant may be found, resides, has an agent, or transacts business."

ops.w: In an action under this subsection, process may be served in the judicial district where the case is brought or any other judicial district of the United States where the defendant may be found, resides, has an agent, or transacts business.

am.cost: The wording follows section 4104(b) of title 28. It widens where a defendant can be served but does not by itself establish that a foreign party has enough contacts with the United States for a court to hear the case.

findings.where: Sec. 2(b), new 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(7), as applied to international organizations
findings.title: Under Jam v. IFC, the GRANITE Act's new immunity exception may also reach international organizations, but only for measures that count as issued by a foreign state.
findings.plain: A separate law protects international bodies, such as some European Union institutions, from being sued. The Supreme Court has said that law gives them the same protection foreign governments have at any given time. So when the GRANITE Act removes foreign governments' protection, it may remove theirs too. The bill still only covers orders from a "foreign state", so the question of whether the European Commission counts as one remains.
findings.tech: Section 2(b) adds 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(7), "under section 4106." In Jam v. International Finance Corp. (2019), the Supreme Court held that "The IOIA affords international organizations the same immunity from suit that foreign governments enjoy today under the FSIA," and that the statute makes "international organization immunity and foreign sovereign immunity continuously equivalent." The Court also stated that "the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act governs the immunity of international organizations." It added that "the organization's charter can always specify a different level of immunity." Read with Jam, a new FSIA exception would apply by default to an organization covered by the International Organizations Immunities Act, unless its charter provides otherwise. That narrows the immunity gap that ITIF identifies (finding R11). It does not settle coverage, because the action must still concern a judgment, fine, order or demand "issued by a foreign court or a foreign state" enforcing a "law of a foreign state" (section 4106(a) and (c)(1)). Whether a given European Union body is designated under the IOIA, and whether its founding instruments specify immunity, was not established for this analysis.
findings.use: A U.S. person suing a European Union body under section 4106(b) can cite Jam to argue that the body's statutory immunity now includes the new exception, while the body can argue its charter or its status outside "foreign state" keeps it out.

s.l: Jam v. International Finance Corp., 586 U.S. ___ (2019)

a.q: No Sovereign Immunity

findings.title: The GRANITE Act's immunity exception has no link to conduct in the United States, unlike the commercial activity and tort exceptions already in the FSIA.
findings.plain: Most existing exceptions to foreign governments' protection from suit require a link to the United States, such as business done here or harm caused here. The new exception has no such link. A foreign government could be sued over an order it issued at home, under its own law. Other countries could treat U.S. agencies the same way.
findings.tech: Existing exceptions in 28 U.S.C. 1605(a) tie jurisdiction to the United States: paragraph (2) covers actions "based upon a commercial activity carried on in the United States" and paragraph (5) covers injury or loss "occurring in the United States." New paragraph (7), "under section 4106", requires only that the action be brought under section 4106, which reaches any judgment, fine, order or demand "issued by a foreign court or a foreign state" and served on a U.S. person. No link to U.S. territory, commerce or enforcement is required. The FSIA does already contain exceptions without a territorial link, such as section 1605A, which is limited to a foreign state "designated as a state sponsor of terrorism" by the executive branch. The 4chan court's statement that immunity is "motivated in part by a desire for reciprocity" (finding R8) identifies the retaliation concern.
findings.use: A foreign government sued under section 4106(b) can argue that the absence of any U.S. connection calls for a narrow reading of the exception, and its own legislature can cite the exception when narrowing U.S. immunity in its courts.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 1605 (general exceptions to foreign state immunity), Office of the Law Revision Counsel
28 U.S.C. 1605A (terrorism exception)

findings.title: The GRANITE Act's compelled disclosure clause could reach foreign evidence and data requests, and the bill does not address evidence treaties or CLOUD Act agreements.
findings.plain: The bill covers foreign laws that force people to hand over information in a way that discourages speech. Foreign subpoenas, data requests and evidence requests could fall under that wording. The United States has signed agreements on sharing evidence and data with other countries, and the bill does not say how it fits with them.
findings.tech: Clause (A)(iii) of section 4106(c)(1) reaches a law that "compels disclosure that would reasonably chill" expression, and section 4106(a) reaches a foreign "order, or demand". As written, this could include foreign subpoenas, data production orders, tax or anti-money-laundering requests, and requests for evidence, subject to the First Amendment test in clause (B). The United States has been a party to the 1970 Hague Evidence Convention since ratification on August 8, 1972 (in force October 7, 1972). Executive agreements under the CLOUD Act already require that "an order issued by the foreign government may not be used to infringe freedom of speech" (18 U.S.C. 2523(b)(4)(E)). Section 4106 mentions neither, and does not say whether it limits U.S. court assistance under those instruments. Where cooperation runs through the executive branch rather than through a court's recognition or enforcement, finding R9 applies. On recognition of judgments, the United States signed the 2019 Hague Judgments Convention on March 2, 2022 but has not ratified it, so no judgments treaty currently conflicts with section 4106(a).
findings.use: A foreign authority seeking evidence from a U.S. source can route its request through the Hague Evidence Convention or a CLOUD Act agreement and argue that section 4106 does not reach it. A U.S. person can argue that a chilling disclosure order is a "demand" enforcing a foreign censorship law.

s.l: 18 U.S.C. 2523 (CLOUD Act executive agreements)

a.q: has the primary purpose or substantial effect of

findings.title: Clause (A) of the GRANITE Act's definition reaches any foreign law with a substantial effect on expression, so clause (B) does most of the narrowing.
findings.plain: The first half of the definition covers any foreign law that has a big effect on speech, even if that is not its main goal. That could include fraud, securities, consumer protection, trade secret, copyright and court gag order rules. Only the second half, the First Amendment test, screens these out. Many would pass that test, since U.S. law does not protect fraud, but each case would turn on a court's analysis.
findings.tech: Clause (A)(i) of section 4106(c)(1) covers a law that "has the primary purpose or substantial effect of restricting or penalizing expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association". The "substantial effect" alternative reaches laws whose aim is not speech regulation, such as fraud and consumer protection rules, securities disclosure rules, copyright and trademark law, trade secret and confidentiality enforcement, court gag orders, and child safety and terrorist content rules. Clause (B) then excludes laws that would not conflict with the First Amendment. Many such laws would be excluded: the Supreme Court stated in Illinois ex rel. Madigan v. Telemarketing Associates (2003) that "the First Amendment does not shield fraud." The practical scope therefore depends on how courts apply clause (B), which finding R1 addresses, and on whether the whole statute or the provision applied is tested.
findings.use: A U.S. party resisting a foreign commercial judgment, such as one based on confidentiality or disclosure rules, can argue that the underlying law has a substantial effect on expression and so meets clause (A), leaving the dispute to clause (B).

s.l: Illinois ex rel. Madigan v. Telemarketing Associates, 538 U.S. 600 (2003)

findings.title: The GRANITE Act asks whether a foreign law would conflict with the First Amendment "if recognized", and leaves every state and federal court to apply that test its own way.
findings.plain: Courts usually recognize foreign court rulings, not foreign laws, so the bill's phrase about a law being "recognized in the United States" is an unusual fit. The bill gives no method for applying the test. State and federal courts could reach different answers, so the same foreign order might be enforceable in one state and not in another until higher courts settle the question.
findings.tech: Clause (B) of section 4106(c)(1) asks whether a foreign law "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution if recognized in the United States." Recognition is ordinarily something a court does to a judgment, as section 4106(a) itself uses the word ("shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment"). The phrase is most naturally read as asking whether the foreign rule would be unconstitutional if it were U.S. law, but the text does not say so. Section 4106(a) binds every "domestic court", which 28 U.S.C. 4101 defines to include state courts. Because each state and federal court applies the test for itself, the same foreign measure could be treated differently in different courts until appellate courts settle the method. This consequence is inferred from the text.
findings.use: A party seeking enforcement can choose a forum whose courts read clause (B) narrowly, and a party resisting it can argue for the hypothetical U.S. law reading.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4101 (SPEECH Act definitions)

a.q: Chapter 181 of title 28, United States Code, is amended by inserting after the item relating to section 4105

findings.title: The GRANITE Act's clerical amendment directs a change to chapter 181 itself, when the item it adds belongs in that chapter's table of sections.
findings.plain: The last part of the bill adds the new section's name to a list of sections. It tells the reader to change the chapter, not the list. Those who compile the law would likely fix this, but it is a small drafting error.
findings.tech: Section 2(c) states: "Chapter 181 of title 28, United States Code, is amended by inserting after the item relating to section 4105 the following". The House Legislative Counsel's Manual on Drafting Style, section 332(f), states that "The elements of a table of contents, or any other table, are generally referred to as 'items'" "for purposes of amendments or cross references." An "item relating to section 4105" exists only in the table of sections at the head of chapter 181. The SPEECH Act, which created chapter 181, directed its own clerical amendment to the table: "The table of chapters for part VI of title 28, United States Code, is amended by adding at the end the following" (Pub. L. 111-223, section 3(c)). The instruction would read correctly as "The table of sections for chapter 181 of title 28, United States Code, is amended".
findings.use: None of substance; the Office of the Law Revision Counsel would likely execute the amendment to the table as intended.

findings.title: The GRANITE Act has no severability clause, but courts presume that an invalid provision can be cut from the rest of a law.
findings.plain: The bill does not say what happens if a court strikes down one part of it. That kind of silence is common. The Supreme Court presumes that the rest of a law survives when one part fails, even without such a clause.
findings.tech: The bill contains no severability or nonseverability clause. In Barr v. American Association of Political Consultants (2020), the plurality stated that "The Court's cases have instead developed a strong presumption of severability." It also stated that "The Court presumes that an unconstitutional provision in a law is severable from the remainder of the law or statute," and noted that "Congress often does not include either a severability clause or a nonseverability clause." If, for example, the immunity exception or the declaratory action were held invalid, the bar in section 4106(a) would likely remain. This is a limit shared by most bills of this type.
findings.use: A party that challenges one provision cannot rely on the absence of a severability clause to bring down the whole Act.

s.l: Barr v. American Assn. of Political Consultants, 591 U.S. ___ (2020)

findings.title: The GRANITE Act's bar on enforcement has no exception for foreign judgments or settlements a U.S. party agreed to, such as consent judgments or contract-based forum choices.
findings.plain: Sometimes an American company agrees to a court order abroad, or signs a contract choosing a foreign court. The bill has no exception for these. A U.S. court could be barred from enforcing a ruling the American side accepted, if it enforces a foreign speech law.
findings.tech: Section 4106(a) provides that "Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal or State law, a domestic court shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment, or a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state, enforcing a foreign censorship law." It contains no exception for judgments entered by consent, settlements, or judgments from a forum the U.S. party chose by contract. The bill also lists no exceptions for categories such as child sexual abuse material, true threats, incitement or fraud; for those, clause (B) does the work, subject to the whole statute question in finding R1. Whether the bar reaches consent judgments depends on whether a judgment entered by agreement is one "enforcing" the foreign law, which the text does not address.
findings.use: A U.S. party that agreed to a foreign judgment or settlement on content obligations can later resist its enforcement in a U.S. court by invoking section 4106(a).

findings.title: The GRANITE Act gives the President and State Department no waiver, certification or other role in suits it allows against foreign governments.
findings.plain: The bill lets Americans sue foreign governments without any step by the President or State Department. Some other exceptions to foreign governments' protection depend on a State Department decision. The Justice Department can still take part in a case to state the government's view, but it cannot stop one.
findings.tech: Neither section 4106 nor new section 1605(a)(7) provides a national security or foreign policy waiver, an executive certification, or a stay for diplomatic negotiation. By contrast, the terrorism exception applies only where "the foreign state was designated as a state sponsor of terrorism" (28 U.S.C. 1605A(a)(2)(A)(i)(I)), a determination the executive makes. Under existing law the Attorney General may send an officer "to attend to the interests of the United States in a suit pending" in a federal or state court (28 U.S.C. 517), so the executive branch can file its views in a section 4106 case. It has no power under the bill to prevent or pause one.
findings.use: A U.S. person can sue a foreign government under section 4106(b) without executive approval, and the executive branch can only advise the court through a statement of interest.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 1605A (terrorism exception)
28 U.S.C. 517 (interests of United States in pending suits)

findings.pat: Title does not match operative text

a.q: Novel International Tyranny and Extortion

findings.title: The GRANITE Act's short title refers to "Extortion", but no operative provision mentions or defines extortion.
findings.plain: The bill's full name speaks of foreign "tyranny and extortion". The rules in the bill only deal with foreign speech laws and court enforcement. Nothing in the bill defines or addresses extortion.
findings.tech: Section 1 provides that the Act may be cited as the "Guaranteeing Rights Against Novel International Tyranny and Extortion Act". The operative text in sections 2(a) to 2(c) uses the terms "foreign censorship law", "judgment", "fine, order, or demand" and "declaratory relief", and does not use "extortion" or "tyranny". A short title has no operative effect, so the word changes no outcome. It frames the bill's purpose in terms the text does not carry.
findings.use: Supporters can describe the bill as an anti-extortion measure, although its operative test is whether a foreign law restricts expression and would conflict with the First Amendment.

s.l: H.R. 10174 introduced text, GovInfo

findings.title: Foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies and outlets registered abroad are not "United States persons" and cannot bring a GRANITE Act suit.
findings.plain: Only a "United States person" can sue under the bill. For a business, that means one formed in or based in the United States. A U.S. company's branch formed abroad, or a news site an American runs through a foreign company, cannot sue, even though the bar on enforcement still protects them in U.S. courts.
findings.tech: The bar in section 4106(a) applies whoever the target is, but the right of action in section 4106(b) belongs only to "A United States person". 28 U.S.C. 4101(6)(D) covers "a business entity incorporated in, or with its primary location or place of operation in, the United States." A subsidiary incorporated and operating abroad, or a publication run through a foreign-registered company, falls outside that clause. Foreign regulators often act against a U.S. company's local subsidiary (finding R4), and that subsidiary has no claim of its own.
findings.use: A foreign regulator can direct an order at a U.S. company's locally incorporated subsidiary, which cannot sue under section 4106(b).

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4101 (SPEECH Act definitions)

findings.title: Because a mere foreign "demand" that is "purportedly served" allows a GRANITE Act suit, foreign governments may often be named as defendants in U.S. courts.
findings.plain: The bill lets an American sue after receiving even an informal foreign demand, or one that was not properly delivered. That low bar could lead to many suits against foreign governments. That could add to diplomatic friction and to court workload, though standing rules may screen out some cases.
findings.tech: Section 4106(b) allows a suit by a U.S. person "upon whom a judgment, fine, order, or demand described in subsection (a) is served or purportedly served", and "demand" is undefined (finding R9). With the FSIA exception in section 2(b), the threshold for naming a foreign state as a defendant is lower than under other exceptions. A plain AI review states that this could make foreign governments frequent defendants and add to diplomatic friction and court workload. Standing and ripeness limits (finding R3) may screen out suits over informal requests. This point has not been verified against a primary source.
findings.use: A U.S. recipient of an informal foreign regulatory letter can file a section 4106(b) action naming the foreign state, forcing it to appear or to contest jurisdiction.

questions.q: What can a foreign regulator do to a United States service today that it could not do after the GRANITE Act took effect?
questions.a: It could no longer defeat a United States declaratory suit by claiming immunity, though standing and comity defenses remain. Collecting a fine through United States courts is already unavailable under existing law. Fines, blocking, orders to intermediaries and action against staff or assets abroad are unaffected.

s.l: Huntington v. Attrill, 146 U.S. 657 (1892)

questions.q: Section 4106(c)(1)(B) asks whether a foreign law "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment". Is that a test of the whole foreign statute or of the provision that the ruling applied?
questions.a: The bill does not say. The SPEECH Act tests the law applied in the foreign adjudication, while First Amendment overbreadth doctrine would look at a statute's full sweep. Under a whole-statute reading, even an order about child sexual abuse material under an overbroad statute could be refused.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4102 (SPEECH Act recognition rules)
United States v. Stevens, 559 U.S. 460 (2010)

questions.q: Which foreign bodies are a "foreign state" under section 1603?
questions.a: Countries, their political subdivisions, and their agencies and instrumentalities, such as the UK's Ofcom. The Second Circuit has held that the European Community is an organ of a foreign state under the same definition, and the Fifth Circuit has treated entities owned jointly by several states as covered.

s.l: European Community v. RJR Nabisco (2d Cir. 2014)
Mangattu v. M/V Ibn Hayyan, 35 F.3d 205 (5th Cir. 1994)

questions.q: What does a United States person who wins a GRANITE Act suit receive?
questions.a: A declaration that the foreign ruling is unenforceable under section 4106(a). There are no damages and no attorney's fees. Competing proposals add both, and any award would be owed by the foreign state.

questions.q: How does section 4106 fit with the SPEECH Act, sections 4101 to 4105 of the same chapter?
questions.a: It borrows the SPEECH Act's definitions and extends its approach beyond defamation and beyond court judgments. For defamation, it appears to override the SPEECH Act's route for enforcing judgments against defendants who would have been liable in the United States. The SPEECH Act's fee and removal rules do not carry over.

questions.q: Could a United States platform sued by its own user for removing content defend itself by pointing to a foreign order that required the removal?
questions.a: Section 4106(a) bars a domestic court from recognizing a foreign order enforcing a foreign censorship law, which could be read to bar recognizing it even as a defense. That reading is untested. A platform would more often rely on its terms of service and section 230 of the Communications Act.

questions.q: What happened in United States courts when American companies sued foreign regulators before this bill?
questions.a: 4chan's suit against Ofcom was dismissed in September 2026 because Ofcom is immune under the FSIA. The judge noted that Congress could subject foreign governments to suit if it wished. Trump Media and Rumble's suit against a Brazilian justice is pending, with Brazil asserting immunity.

questions.q: Does "any law of a foreign state" in section 4106(c)(1) include regulations, regulators' decisions, codes of practice and judge-made rules?
questions.a: The text does not say. Section 4106(c)(1) uses "any law of a foreign state" and does not define "law". The SPEECH Act definitions that section 4106 borrows treat a "foreign court" as "a court, administrative body, or other tribunal of a foreign country". A regulator's final decision can therefore be a "foreign judgment", but that definition does not decide which foreign rules count as "law". cls.function: A bill that adds a court rule and a new exception to the law that protects foreign governments from lawsuits
cls.banner: This is a bill in Congress. It is not law. If passed, it would stop federal and state courts from enforcing foreign court rulings, fines and orders. This covers rulings that punish speech the First Amendment protects. That part of the Constitution protects free speech. An American who gets such an order could ask a federal court to declare it unenforceable. That includes a suit against a foreign government.
cls.checks: Every type of check was run on this bill. The bill changes laws that already exist. So the review first looked at how it fits with those laws. One is the SPEECH Act, a law about foreign libel rulings. Another is the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. The review also looked at the fixes those laws give people and at what their words mean.

stated.t: To amend title 28, United States Code, to limit the enforcement of foreign censorship judgments, and for other purposes.

marketed.t: Rep. Rulli told The Times that a foreign judgment over protected speech would be "dead on arrival in our courts."
marketed.l: Free Speech Union, citing The Times

marketed.t: Rep. Rulli wrote that the bill would "defend our digital sovereignty and protect Americans from foreign censorship attempts."
Rep. Rulli said: "The constitution protects our right to speak freely. It does not bend to Brussels or London."

ladder.mechanism: The bill would stop American courts from enforcing foreign rulings that back speech-limiting laws. It would let an American ask a court to say such a ruling cannot be enforced. It would also take away a foreign government's protection from being sued in that case.
ladder.outcome: The goal is that foreign governments and regulators cannot use American courts. They could not collect fines or enforce orders over speech that the First Amendment protects.
ladder.aim: The bigger aim is free speech online. Americans and American companies could speak and publish without having to follow foreign speech rules.

a.q: would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution if recognized in the United States

findings.title: The bill does not say if a "foreign censorship law" means a whole foreign law or only the part used.
findings.plain: The bill blocks rulings that enforce a foreign law that would conflict with the First Amendment. It does not say how much counts as the law. It could mean a whole law, or only the rule used in the case. A broad foreign law with one part that conflicts could be treated either way.
findings.tech: The bill defines a foreign censorship law as "any law of a foreign state" with a speech-restricting purpose or effect. The law must be one that "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment ... if recognized in the United States." That is the bill's test. The bill bars rulings "enforcing a foreign censorship law." The text does not say what "law" means. It could mean a whole law. It could mean one part of a law. It could mean a rule as applied to the speaker. Courts would likely look at the part the ruling enforced. That is by analogy to the SPEECH Act. That Act tests "the defamation law applied in the foreign court's adjudication". That reading is an inference. A court could instead apply a First Amendment test called overbreadth. That test means that "a substantial number of its applications are unconstitutional, judged in relation to the statute's plainly legitimate sweep". A law that fails it falls. Here "statute" means a law. The words "legitimate sweep" mean its valid reach. The Supreme Court used that wording in United States v. Stevens, which was decided in 2010. Under that test, a court could refuse a ruling under a too-broad foreign law. That could happen even if the conduct would not be protected in the United States. The definition makes no exceptions. It also reaches foreign privacy and data protection orders, harassment orders, laws on nonconsensual intimate images and intellectual property law. Each depends on the same First Amendment test. A rival bill, the HOMEFRONT Act, looks at the one case. It blocks a foreign ruling unless the court finds the conduct would not have been protected by the First Amendment.
findings.use: A person fighting a foreign ruling can argue that the whole foreign law is too broad. That holds even if the speech involved is not protected in the United States. A person seeking enforcement can argue that only the part used counts, and that it is valid.

findings.title: The bill could block foreign libel rulings the SPEECH Act allows when the defendant would lose in an American court.
findings.plain: A 2010 law, the SPEECH Act, lets American courts enforce a foreign libel ruling in two cases. One is when the foreign law protected speech as much as American law. The other is when the person would have lost in an American court anyway. The new rule applies over other laws and has no second route, so it could block rulings the older law allows.
findings.tech: The SPEECH Act lets an American court enforce a foreign libel ruling if the side seeking enforcement shows one of two things. The first route is that the foreign libel law protected speech at least as much as the First Amendment. The second route is liability "even if the defamation law applied in the foreign court's adjudication did not provide as much protection". That means the defendant would have lost under American standards. A foreign libel law that fails the First Amendment also meets the bill's definition of a foreign censorship law. The bill applies "Notwithstanding any other provision of Federal or State law", which means it overrides other laws. It has no second route like the SPEECH Act has. Read together, the bill appears to bar enforcement where the SPEECH Act would allow it. This interaction is inferred from the text, and no source has addressed it. The bill also borrows the SPEECH Act's definitions. Under them, a "foreign court" includes an administrative body. So a final decision of a regulator such as Ofcom can be a "foreign judgment".
findings.use: An American author could avoid a foreign ruling that the SPEECH Act would let courts enforce. This covers an author who would have lost a libel case in an American court. One example is the actual malice standard.

findings.title: The GRANITE Act suit may fail if a foreign regulator never tried to enforce its speech order here.
findings.plain: Federal courts can only decide real, present disputes. A foreign regulator that never tries to collect in the United States will say there is nothing to decide. A court may agree. It could dismiss the suit, even though the bill says the suit is allowed.
findings.tech: The bill creates a right to sue. But that may not be enough. In a 2016 case, Spokeo v. Robins, the Supreme Court spoke to this. It said "It is settled that Congress cannot erase Article III's standing requirements by statutorily granting the right to sue". Article III is the part of the Constitution that limits federal courts to real cases. The Supreme Court has set a test in MedImmune v. Genentech in 2007 for suits that seek a declaration. Such a suit must show "a substantial controversy, between parties having adverse legal interests, of sufficient immediacy and reality". A foreign regulator may never seek enforcement here. It can argue there is no immediate dispute. It can also argue that a ruling here fixes nothing. Enforcement happens at home. In February 2025, a court denied emergency relief in Trump Media v. De Moraes. One reason was that the fight over Brazilian orders was not ripe. Ripe means ready for a court to decide. The bill treats service of an order on an American as enough to sue. That may help show a real dispute. How courts would weigh it is unsettled.
findings.use: A foreign regulator sued under the bill can ask the court to dismiss the case. It can say the American has no standing, meaning no right to bring the case. It can also say the case is not ripe. This can happen before any question of immunity comes up. An American who only got a notice may lose on that ground.

findings.tech: The bill limits who can sue. The person must be one "against whom a foreign judgment ... is entered, or upon whom a judgment, fine, order, or demand ... is served or purportedly served". An order sent to a foreign internet provider or an app store is not served on the American speaker. An order sent to a foreign subsidiary of an American company is not served on the American parent company. The bill still bars American courts from enforcing such orders. But there would rarely be an American enforcement case. The affected American has no right to sue.

findings.tech: Ofcom, the UK regulator, sent orders to 4chan. In the words of 4chan's lawyer, they were "information demands" seeking a "risk assessment report". Ofcom's decision of April 21, 2026 found several breaches. They included failing to send the required risk assessment, inadequate terms of service and inadequate age verification. The penalties total 520,000 pounds plus daily fines. One part of the bill's definition covers a law that "compels disclosure that would reasonably chill" expression. To chill means to discourage. That part may reach such demands. A regulator will argue that a penalty for failing to answer a request or file a report is only a procedural sanction. That means a penalty for skipping a step. It will say that this does not restrict expression at all. The bill does not address procedural or reporting penalties directly.

So foreign rules that require age checks may fall outside it. Age checks are a major part of the UK law that inspired the bill.
findings.tech: In 2025 the Supreme Court decided Free Speech Coalition v. Paxton. The case was about a Texas law requiring age checks on some sexually explicit websites. It held "that the correct tier of review was intermediate scrutiny" for that law. Intermediate scrutiny is a middle level of court review. The Court also ruled that the law "readily satisfie[d]" it. One part of the bill's definition asks if a foreign law "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment". A foreign age check rule like the Texas law would likely not conflict. So orders enforcing it would fall outside the bill. Ofcom's decision against 4chan included a breach of the Online Safety Act's age verification duty. The bill does not say if age checks are in or out. It is unsettled how far the Paxton holding reaches beyond sexually explicit content.
findings.use: A foreign regulator can enforce age check duties against American services. It can say these duties are not censorship laws under the bill. It can point to the Paxton case.

a.q: seeking declaratory relief

findings.title: Under the bill, Americans can win a ruling against foreign speech orders. They cannot win money or legal fees.
findings.plain: An American who gets a foreign fine or order over protected speech can ask a federal court for a ruling. The ruling would say that American courts will not enforce it. The bill gives no money damages and does not repay legal fees. That is a choice, and other proposals add money, which has its own costs.
findings.tech: The bill allows only a suit "seeking declaratory relief". That means a suit that asks for a ruling. A declaration applies the bar to one foreign measure. It can come before anyone seeks enforcement. It gives the American a binding ruling. The American can show it to banks, payment processors and hosting providers. The bill has no rule on legal fees. The SPEECH Act has a fee rule and a rule on moving cases to federal court. They apply only to suits on foreign libel rulings. So they do not carry over. The HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, allows more. It allows a ruling and a court order to stop enforcement. It also allows attorney's fees and $25,000 in damages set by law. ITIF proposed damages of $1 million per violation or 10 percent of United States-related revenue. R Street warned that damages set by law can bear no relation to the harm suffered. Any money award would be owed by the foreign state, not the United States. Under a federal law, a foreign state's property in the United States is "immune from attachment arrest and execution". Two other rules create exceptions.
findings.use: An American who wins a suit under the bill still pays their own legal costs. That weighs most on small publishers. Damages would raise the stakes for foreign governments, but the awards would be hard to collect.

findings.title: The bill ends foreign governments' protection from suit with one short phrase. Slow service rules and other defenses remain.
findings.plain: The bill ends foreign governments' protection from being sued in these cases. It does this with one short phrase. It does nothing about the slow formal process for serving papers on a foreign government. Foreign governments can still raise other defenses. A federal judge has said this protection exists partly so other countries treat America the same way.
findings.tech: The bill adds a short phrase to the federal law on foreign immunity from suit. It removes immunity and nothing else. Papers served on a foreign state must follow a separate federal law. If needed, the Secretary of State sends them "through diplomatic channels". The state then has 60 days to answer. The phrase does not deal with the act of state defense. It also does not deal with courts holding back out of comity, meaning respect between countries. The court that dismissed 4chan's suit said foreign sovereign immunity is granted "as a matter of grace and comity". It also said immunity is "motivated in part by a desire for reciprocity". Reciprocity means other countries give the same protection in return. Defendants can cite that reasoning to argue for a narrow reading of the new exception. It also names the reciprocity risk Congress weighs when it removes immunity. The immunity of individual foreign officials is also untouched. The Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act does not govern it. That matters little when the only remedy is a declaration against the state.
findings.use: A foreign government sued under the bill can slow the case through the rules on serving papers. It can then raise comity or the act of state defense. It can also ask the court to read the new exception narrowly because of reciprocity.

a.q: a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state

findings.title: The bill does not define "demand". It also leaves out agency help, extradition and evidence help in foreign speech cases.
findings.plain: The bill does not say what counts as a foreign "demand". An emailed request or a voluntary code are examples. The bill only stops courts from enforcing foreign rulings. American agencies can still cooperate with foreign speech cases. American courts can still help foreign courts gather evidence.
findings.tech: The bill covers "a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state". It does not define "demand". So it is unclear if some things count. One is an emailed request. One is a voluntary code of conduct. One is a notice from a flagging organization that a government recognizes. The bar applies only to a court that would "recognize or enforce" a foreign measure. A federal law lets a district court order testimony or documents "for use in a proceeding in a foreign or international tribunal". A court that does this is arguably not recognizing or enforcing anything. The bill does not address treaties that let governments help each other in legal cases. It does not address extradition decisions either. The writer of the original GRANITE idea says those protections are not explicit in the bill. Wyoming's bill barred state agencies and employees from "cooperating with foreign censorship orders or extradition requests based on speech-related offenses". The HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, bars officials from helping foreign enforcement. It also bars extradition for protected conduct.

a.q: a domestic court shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment

findings.title: Courts already refuse foreign government fines. The GRANITE Act adds suits against foreign governments and a bar on private awards.
findings.plain: American courts have long refused to collect fines for foreign governments. So the bill's ban on enforcing foreign speech fines mostly writes down an old rule. Its new effects are letting Americans sue foreign governments over these orders. It also blocks foreign court awards that private people win under speech laws.
findings.tech: The Supreme Court stated in Huntington v. Attrill in 1892 that "The courts of no country execute the penal laws of another." Penal laws are laws that punish. State laws are based on a uniform act on foreign money judgments. Those laws exclude any judgment that is "A fine or other penalty." So such fines are not recognized. The federal court in Washington dismissed 4chan's suit against Ofcom. It observed that "American courts generally decline to enforce foreign judgments that violate the United States Constitution". It also observed that American courts "are not necessarily required to enforce foreign penal judgments." Those are judgments that punish. Ofcom's chief executive spoke to members of Parliament. Only two of eleven Online Safety Act fines had been paid. A report of the same evidence states that four sites had geo-blocked the United Kingdom. That means they blocked access from there. In February 2025, a federal court in Florida denied Rumble and Trump Media an emergency order against a Brazilian justice's directives. It found that the directives had not been served under the Hague Convention. It also found they were not served under the United States-Brazil treaty on mutual legal assistance. So the directives imposed no obligation to comply. Against that background, the bill's new legal elements are two. One is the exception to foreign immunity. It lets an American sue a foreign state for a declaration. The other is a written bar on private foreign judgments under speech laws other than libel laws. The SPEECH Act already covers libel judgments. For those, the bill changes the result as another finding in this review describes. Courts now assess private foreign judgments under other speech laws. They use the public policy ground in state recognition laws. That ground lets a court refuse a judgment "repugnant to the public policy of this State or the United States."
findings.use: Supporters can say the bill stops foreign governments from collecting speech fines in American courts. Those courts already refuse to do that. The real changes are suits against foreign governments in American courts. Another change is a firmer, uniform bar on private parties' foreign judgments under speech laws.

a.q: enforcing a foreign censorship law

findings.title: The bill never says who must prove a law is a "foreign censorship law", which matters most for private awards.
findings.plain: Someone has to show that the foreign law punishes protected speech. The bill does not say who. Judges decide most of that as a legal question, so the missing answer matters less than it seems. It matters most when a private person tries to collect a foreign court award.
findings.tech: Two questions matter here. One is whether a foreign law restricts expression. The other is whether it conflicts with the First Amendment. Both are largely questions of law. A federal rule says a court deciding foreign law "may consider any relevant material or source". The court's decision "must be treated as a ruling on a question of law." Foreign government fines already cannot be enforced here. The choice of who carries the burden matters most for money judgments that private parties win under foreign speech laws. State laws based on the uniform foreign-money-judgments act say this. They say "A party resisting recognition of a foreign-country judgment has the burden of establishing" a ground for not recognizing it. So the American defendant would likely carry that burden. The SPEECH Act reverses that rule for libel judgments. How the state rule applies to the bill is inferred. A rival bill, the HOMEFRONT Act, puts that burden on the side trying to collect.
findings.use: A private party may hold a foreign judgment under a foreign speech law against an American. The American would likely have to prove the law is a "foreign censorship law". That is the reverse of the SPEECH Act rule for libel.
