a.q: restricting or penalizing expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association

findings.title: Courts treat how platforms sort posts as speech. So the bill may block foreign rules on how platforms moderate.
findings.plain: The Supreme Court has said that a platform's choices about which posts to show are its own speech. So a foreign rule telling a platform how to moderate could count as a speech law under the bill. The bill could then protect large platforms from foreign platform rules in general, not only people who post.
findings.tech: The bill covers laws that limit "expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association". It does not define those words. The Supreme Court looked at how platforms pick and order posts in a 2024 case, Moody v. NetChoice, about state laws. It said "they are making expressive choices". That means the choices are the platform's own speech. The Court also said "a State may not interfere with private actors' speech to advance its own vision of ideological balance". So a foreign law that makes a platform remove kinds of posts or change its rankings may limit the platform's own speech. If an American law did the same thing, it could break the First Amendment. The bill could then reach foreign rules on platform design and moderation in general. No court has tested this, so this reading is an inference.
findings.use: A foreign government may tell a large platform to reduce risks on its service. The platform can argue that the rule limits its own speech. It can then argue the rule is a "foreign censorship law".

s.l: Moody v. NetChoice, LLC, 603 U.S. 707 (2024)

a.q: Right Of Action

findings.title: The bill never says whom an American sues. A suit against a private foreign party may fail.
findings.plain: The bill lets an American sue but never says whom. Often the other side is a private person or company abroad that won a ruling there. The older libel law lets Americans serve papers anywhere in the country, and this bill does not. A court may then lack power over that foreign party.
findings.tech: The bill allows "an action in an appropriate district court of the United States". It does not name who is sued. The change to the immunity law suggests a foreign government. But private people and companies win many foreign speech rulings. The SPEECH Act has a rule for its own suits. It lets court papers be served in the district where the case is brought. It also allows any other district where the other side can be found, lives, has an agent or does business. This bill has no such rule. A foreign private party that won a ruling abroad, and has done nothing in America, may be beyond an American court's reach. That result is inferred from the missing rule.
findings.use: A foreign party that won a speech ruling abroad can fight an American's suit. It can challenge how papers were served and the court's power over it. The American then gets no ruling until someone tries to collect.

findings.where: Sec. 2(b), new 28 U.S.C. 1605(a)(7), as applied to international organizations
findings.title: The bill may let people sue some international groups too, but only over orders from a foreign state.
findings.plain: A separate law protects international bodies, such as some European Union institutions, from being sued. The Supreme Court has said that law gives them the same protection foreign governments have at any given time. So when the GRANITE Act removes foreign governments' protection, it may remove theirs too. The bill still covers only orders from a "foreign state". Whether the European Commission counts as one remains open.
findings.tech: A separate law gives international organizations protection from suit. In Jam v. International Finance Corp. (2019), the Supreme Court ruled on that law. It said the law gives them "the same immunity from suit that foreign governments enjoy today under the FSIA". The FSIA is the main law that shields foreign governments from lawsuits. The Court added that "the organization's charter can always specify a different level of immunity". So the new exception would apply to such a group by default, unless its charter says otherwise. That narrows the gap in protection that ITIF describes in another finding in this review. It does not settle coverage. The suit must still concern a judgment, fine, order or demand "issued by a foreign court or a foreign state". It must also enforce a "law of a foreign state". This analysis did not establish whether a given European Union body is covered by that separate law. It also did not establish whether the body's founding documents set a level of protection.
findings.use: An American who sues a European Union body can cite the Jam case to say the new exception now applies to it. The body can argue that its charter, or its status outside "foreign state", keeps it out.

s.l: Jam v. International Finance Corp., 586 U.S. ___ (2019)

a.q: No Sovereign Immunity

findings.title: The bill lets people sue a foreign government even when the case has no link to the U.S.
findings.plain: Most existing exceptions to foreign governments' protection from suit require a link to the United States. Examples are business done here or harm caused here. The new exception has no such link. A foreign government could be sued over an order it issued at home, under its own law. Other countries could treat U.S. agencies the same way.
findings.tech: Older exceptions in the law tie a lawsuit to the United States. One covers cases "based upon a commercial activity carried on in the United States". Another covers injury or loss "occurring in the United States". The new exception needs only that the suit is brought under the bill's new rule. That rule reaches any judgment, fine, order or demand "issued by a foreign court or a foreign state". It must also be served on a U.S. person. Nothing ties it to U.S. land, trade or enforcement. Some existing exceptions do lack a link to U.S. territory. One example is the exception limited to a foreign state "designated as a state sponsor of terrorism" by the executive branch. The 4chan court said that immunity is "motivated in part by a desire for reciprocity", as another finding in this review notes. That points to the worry about retaliation.
findings.use: A foreign government sued under the bill can argue that the missing U.S. link calls for a narrow reading. Its own lawmakers can cite the exception when they limit U.S. protection from suit in their courts.

findings.title: The bill could cover foreign data requests, but it does not address CLOUD Act deals or evidence treaties.
findings.plain: The bill covers foreign laws that force people to hand over information if that would discourage speech. Foreign subpoenas, data requests and evidence requests could fall under that wording. The United States has signed agreements on sharing evidence and data with other countries. The bill does not say how it fits with them.
findings.tech: The bill covers a foreign law that "compels disclosure that would reasonably chill" expression. It also covers a foreign "order, or demand". As written, this could include foreign subpoenas, orders to produce data, tax or anti-money-laundering requests, and requests for evidence. Each would still face the First Amendment test. The United States joined the 1970 Hague Evidence Convention by ratifying it on August 8, 1972. It has been in force since October 7, 1972. This treaty covers getting evidence across borders. Executive agreements under the CLOUD Act are deals with other countries. They already require that "an order issued by the foreign government may not be used to infringe freedom of speech". The bill mentions neither, and does not say whether it limits help from U.S. courts under them. Where cooperation runs through the executive branch and not through a court, another finding in this review applies. The United States signed the 2019 Hague Judgments Convention on March 2, 2022 but has not ratified it. So no treaty on judgments now conflicts with the bill.
findings.use: A foreign authority seeking evidence from a U.S. source can use the Hague Evidence Convention or a CLOUD Act deal. It can argue the bill does not reach its request. A U.S. person can argue that a chilling disclosure order is a "demand" enforcing a foreign censorship law.

a.q: has the primary purpose or substantial effect of

findings.title: Foreign laws with a big effect on speech are covered, so the First Amendment test does most of the narrowing.
findings.plain: The first half of the definition covers any foreign law with a big effect on speech. This is true even if speech is not its main goal. That could include fraud, securities, consumer protection, trade secret, copyright and court gag order rules. Only the second half, the First Amendment test, screens these out. Many such laws would be screened out, since U.S. law does not protect fraud. Still, each case would turn on a court's analysis.
findings.tech: The first half covers a law with a certain purpose or effect. Its words are "has the primary purpose or substantial effect of restricting or penalizing expression, expressive conduct, or expressive association". The "substantial effect" part reaches laws that are not aimed at speech. Examples are fraud, consumer protection, securities disclosure, copyright, trademark, trade secret and confidentiality rules. It also reaches court gag orders and child safety and terrorist content rules. The second half then excludes laws that would not conflict with the First Amendment. The Supreme Court stated in Illinois ex rel. Madigan v. Telemarketing Associates (2003) that "the First Amendment does not shield fraud." The real reach depends on how courts apply that second half. Another finding in this review addresses that. It also depends on whether the whole law or only the part applied is tested.
findings.use: A U.S. party resisting a foreign commercial judgment can argue that the law has a big effect on speech. An example is a judgment based on confidentiality or disclosure rules. That meets the first half of the definition. The dispute then turns on the First Amendment test.

s.l: Illinois ex rel. Madigan v. Telemarketing Associates, 538 U.S. 600 (2003)

findings.title: The bill lets each court decide alone if a foreign law would conflict with the First Amendment "if recognized".
findings.plain: Courts usually recognize foreign court rulings, not foreign laws. So the bill's phrase about a law being "recognized in the United States" is an unusual fit. The bill gives no method for applying the test. State and federal courts could reach different answers. The same foreign order might be enforceable in one state and not in another until higher courts decide.
findings.tech: The bill asks if a foreign law "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment of the United States Constitution". It adds the words "if recognized in the United States." Recognition is ordinarily something a court does to a judgment. The bill itself uses the word that way when it says a court "shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment". The phrase most naturally asks if the foreign rule would be unconstitutional if it were U.S. law. The bill does not say so. The bar binds every "domestic court", which the law defines to include state courts. Each court applies the test for itself, so the same foreign measure could be treated differently until appeals courts settle the method. This result is inferred from the text.
findings.use: A party seeking enforcement can choose a place to sue where the courts read the test narrowly. A party resisting enforcement can argue that the test asks what would happen if the foreign rule were a U.S. law.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4101 (SPEECH Act definitions)

findings.title: If a court strikes down part of the bill, courts presume the rest stands, even without a clause saying so.
findings.plain: The bill does not say what happens if a court strikes down one part of it. That kind of silence is common. The Supreme Court presumes that the rest of a law survives when one part fails, even without such a clause.
findings.tech: The bill has no clause saying whether its parts can be separated. In Barr v. American Association of Political Consultants (2020), the plurality spoke of how courts treat a bad part of a law. It noted a "strong presumption of severability", meaning a bad part can be cut away. The plurality also noted that Congress often includes no clause either way. If a court held the immunity exception or the declaratory action invalid, the bar on enforcement would likely remain. Most bills of this type share this limit.
findings.use: A party that challenges one part of the law cannot use the missing clause to bring down the whole law.

s.l: Barr v. American Assn. of Political Consultants, 591 U.S. ___ (2020)

findings.title: The bill bars U.S. courts from enforcing foreign speech rulings, even ones an American agreed to.
findings.plain: Sometimes an American company agrees to a court order abroad, or signs a contract choosing a foreign court. The bill has no exception for these. A U.S. court could be barred from enforcing a ruling the American side accepted, if it enforces a foreign speech law.
findings.tech: The bill says that "a domestic court shall not recognize or enforce a foreign judgment". The bar also covers "a fine, order, or demand issued by a foreign court or a foreign state". It applies to those "enforcing a foreign censorship law." It has no exception for judgments entered by consent, for settlements, or for judgments from a court the American chose by contract. It also lists no exceptions for child sexual abuse material, true threats, incitement or fraud. For those, the First Amendment test does the work. Another finding in this review asks whether the whole law is tested. Whether the bar reaches consent judgments depends on whether a judgment entered by agreement is one "enforcing" the foreign law. The bill does not address that.
findings.use: A U.S. party that agreed to a foreign judgment or settlement about content can later fight enforcement in a U.S. court. It can cite the bar in the bill.

findings.title: The bill lets people sue foreign governments. The President and State Department have no waiver or role.
findings.plain: The bill lets Americans sue foreign governments without any step by the President or State Department. Some other exceptions to foreign governments' protection depend on a State Department decision. The Justice Department can still join a case to state the government's view. It has no power to stop a case.
findings.tech: The bill has no waiver for national security or foreign policy. It has no approval from the executive branch and no pause for talks with another country. The terrorism exception works differently. It applies only where "the foreign state was designated as a state sponsor of terrorism". The executive branch makes that decision. Existing law lets the Attorney General, the top U.S. law enforcement official, send an officer to a federal or state court. The officer's job is "to attend to the interests of the United States in a suit pending". So the executive branch can tell a court its views in a case under the bill. The bill gives it no power to stop or pause a case.
findings.use: An American can sue a foreign government under the bill without asking the executive branch. The executive branch can only advise the court. It does this in a filing called a statement of interest.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 1605A (terrorism exception)
28 U.S.C. 517 (interests of United States in pending suits)

findings.plain: The bill's full name speaks of foreign "tyranny and extortion". The rules in the bill only deal with foreign speech laws and court enforcement. Nothing in the bill defines or addresses extortion.
findings.tech: The bill says it may be cited as the "Guaranteeing Rights Against Novel International Tyranny and Extortion Act". The working text of the bill uses the terms "foreign censorship law", "judgment", "fine, order, or demand" and "declaratory relief". It does not use "extortion" or "tyranny". A short title has no legal effect, so the word changes no outcome. It describes the bill's purpose in terms that the text does not carry.
findings.use: Supporters can describe the bill as an anti-extortion measure. Its actual test is whether a foreign law limits speech and would conflict with the First Amendment.

s.l: H.R. 10174 introduced text, GovInfo

findings.title: Branches of U.S. firms and outlets formed abroad are not "United States persons" and cannot sue under the bill.
findings.plain: Only a "United States person" can sue under the bill. For a business, that means one formed in or based in the United States. A U.S. company's branch formed abroad cannot sue. Neither can a news site an American runs through a foreign company. Still, the bar on enforcement protects them in U.S. courts.
findings.tech: The bar on enforcement covers any target. Only "A United States person" can sue. For a business, the law covers "a business entity incorporated in" the United States. It also covers one "with its primary location or place of operation in, the United States." A branch formed and run abroad is outside that definition. So is a publication run through a foreign-registered company. Foreign regulators often act against a U.S. company's local branch, as another finding in this review notes. That branch has no claim of its own.
findings.use: A foreign regulator can aim an order at a U.S. company's locally formed branch, which cannot sue under the bill.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4101 (SPEECH Act definitions)

findings.title: A foreign "demand" that is "purportedly served" can bring a suit, so foreign states may often be sued.
findings.plain: The bill lets an American sue after receiving even an informal foreign demand, or one that was not properly delivered. That low bar could lead to many suits against foreign governments. That could add to diplomatic friction and to court workload. Rules on who may sue may screen out some cases.
findings.tech: The bill lets a U.S. person sue when a foreign judgment, fine, order or demand "is served or purportedly served". The word "demand" is not defined, as another finding in this review notes. The change to the foreign immunity law makes it easier to name a foreign state as a defendant than under other exceptions. A plain AI review states that this could make foreign governments frequent defendants and add to diplomatic friction and court workload. Limits on who may sue and when may screen out suits over informal requests. This point has not been checked against a source.
findings.use: A U.S. recipient of an informal foreign regulatory letter can file a suit naming the foreign state. That forces the state to appear or to contest the court's power over it.

promises.p: The Times quoted Representative Rulli. He said a foreign ruling over protected speech will be "dead on arrival in our courts".
promises.src: Rep. Rulli, quoted by The Times
promises.why: The bill bars recognizing and enforcing foreign rulings. Whether a ruling falls under the bar depends on two things. One is whether "law" means the whole foreign law or only the part applied. The other is whether penalties for skipped steps, reports and age checks count as censorship.

s.l: Free Speech Union, citing The Times

promises.p: R Street said in a statement that the bill would bar every American court from enforcing foreign censorship rulings. This covers federal and state courts.
promises.why: "Domestic court" means a federal or state court. Federal law says so. The bar applies even if other laws say otherwise. Helping gather evidence is arguably not recognizing or enforcing anything.

s.l: R Street statement on the GRANITE Act

promises.p: Representative Rulli wrote on X that the bill would protect Americans from foreign censorship attempts. Reason quoted him on this.
promises.src: Rep. Rulli on X, quoted by Reason
promises.why: The bill closes American courts to enforcement. A person named or sent the order may sue for a declaration. The bill does not reach orders sent to middlemen such as internet providers. It does not reach agency cooperation. It does not reach enforcement carried out abroad.

s.l: Reason, September 1, 2026

promises.p: Reclaim The Net quoted Representative Rulli. He said the Constitution "does not bend to Brussels or London".
promises.src: Rep. Rulli, quoted by Reclaim The Net
promises.why: UK law and Ofcom are within "foreign state" under the bill. The Second Circuit has held that the European Community is an agency or instrumentality of a foreign state. It used the same definition. Other appeals courts have not settled the question.

s.l: Reclaim The Net on H.R. 10174
European Community v. RJR Nabisco (2d Cir. 2014)

promises.p: Reclaim The Net describes the bill as a way to stop foreign regulators from defeating American suits. It says they do this by claiming sovereign immunity. That means protection from being sued.
promises.why: The bill removes immunity in suits under its new rule. Defenses about standing, ripeness, comity and act of state remain. The exception does not cover claims under other laws.

s.l: Reclaim The Net on H.R. 10174

promises.p: Byrne & Storm are lawyers who responded to the ruling in 4chan v. Ofcom. They said the bill would let Americans get relief in American courts.
promises.src: Byrne & Storm statement on 4chan v. Ofcom
promises.why: The relief is a declaration that a foreign order cannot be enforced. There are no damages or attorney's fees. Only a person named or sent the order can ask for it. It is also subject to the limits Article III of the Constitution puts on federal courts.

s.l: Byrne & Storm statement on the 4chan v. Ofcom ruling, September 15, 2026

questions.q: Foreign regulators can act against online services in America today. What could they not do after the GRANITE Act takes effect?
questions.a: A foreign regulator could no longer use immunity to stop an American suit for a declaration. Defenses about standing and comity would remain. Collecting a fine in American courts is already barred by existing law. The bill does not change fines, blocking or orders to middlemen. It does not change action against staff or assets abroad.

s.l: Huntington v. Attrill, 146 U.S. 657 (1892)

questions.q: The bill asks whether a foreign law "would conflict with the protections of the First Amendment". Is that a test of the whole foreign law or of the part the ruling used?
questions.a: The bill does not say. The SPEECH Act tests the law applied in the foreign court's ruling. The First Amendment overbreadth test would look at a law's full reach. Under a whole-law reading, even an order about child sexual abuse material under a too-broad law could be refused.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4102 (SPEECH Act recognition rules)
United States v. Stevens, 559 U.S. 460 (2010)

questions.q: Which foreign bodies count as a "foreign state" under the bill?
questions.a: A foreign state is a country or one of its local governments. It also includes an agency or other body that acts for it, such as the UK's Ofcom. The Second Circuit has held that the European Community is an organ of a foreign state under the same definition. The Fifth Circuit has treated bodies owned together by several states as covered.

s.l: European Community v. RJR Nabisco (2d Cir. 2014)
Mangattu v. M/V Ibn Hayyan, 35 F.3d 205 (5th Cir. 1994)

questions.q: What does an American who wins a GRANITE Act suit get?
questions.a: The winner gets a declaration that the foreign order cannot be enforced under the bill. The bill gives no damages and no legal fees. Competing proposals add both, and any award would be owed by the foreign government.

questions.q: How does the new rule fit with the SPEECH Act, the older law on foreign libel rulings?
questions.a: It borrows the SPEECH Act's definitions. It goes beyond libel and beyond court judgments. For libel, it appears to override the SPEECH Act's route for enforcing judgments. That route applies to defendants who would have been liable in the United States. The SPEECH Act's fee rules and rules on moving cases to federal court do not carry over.

questions.q: An American platform removed content because a foreign order required it. Can it use that order as a defense if its own user sues?
questions.a: The bill bars an American court from recognizing a foreign order that enforces a foreign censorship law. That could be read to bar recognizing it even as a defense. That reading is untested. A platform would more often rely on its terms of service and on a part of the Communications Act.

questions.q: What happened in court when U.S.-based firms sued foreign regulators before this bill?
questions.a: 4chan's suit against Ofcom was dismissed in September 2026 because Ofcom is immune under the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act. The judge noted that Congress could subject foreign governments to suit if it wished. Trump Media and Rumble's suit against a Brazilian justice is pending. Brazil says it is immune.

s.l: Reuters via WHBL: U.S. court dismisses 4chan's case against Britain's media regulator
Byrne & Storm statement on the 4chan v. Ofcom ruling, September 15, 2026
Civil Rights Litigation Clearinghouse: Trump Media v. De Moraes

questions.q: When would the bill take effect, and would it reach cases that are already pending?
questions.a: It would take effect when it becomes law. That is the usual rule unless a law says otherwise. The Supreme Court has "regularly applied intervening statutes conferring or ousting jurisdiction", meaning new laws on court power apply to pending cases. The Court has also applied the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act to conduct before 1976. A plaintiff in a pending case could add a claim by amending its complaint.

s.l: Gozlon-Peretz v. United States, 498 U.S. 395 (1991)
Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994)
Republic of Austria v. Altmann, 541 U.S. 677 (2004)

questions.q: What do the competing versions of the GRANITE Act add?
questions.a: Senate bill 5478 has the same text. The HOMEFRONT Act, House bill 10309, adds several things. It adds court orders to stop enforcement. It adds attorney's fees. It adds $25,000 in damages set by law. It bars officials from helping foreign enforcement. It bars extradition for protected conduct. It adds a test tied to the Communications Act. Wyoming's bill named international organizations as covered. It also barred state cooperation with foreign censorship orders. It barred cooperation with speech-related extradition requests too.

s.l: S. 5478 text (Sen. Lee), Congress.gov
Preston Byrne on the HOMEFRONT Act, H.R. 10309
Yahoo News: Wyoming bill seeks to stop foreign censorship

questions.q: Does "any law of a foreign state" cover rules set by agencies, by judges or by codes of practice?
questions.a: The bill does not say. It uses "any law of a foreign state" and does not define "law". The bill borrows definitions from the older SPEECH Act. That act treats a "foreign court" as "a court, administrative body, or other tribunal of a foreign country". So a regulator's final decision can be a "foreign judgment". That does not decide which foreign rules count as "law". Courts would have to decide whether codes of practice from a regulator, or rules developed by foreign courts, qualify.

s.l: 28 U.S.C. 4101 (SPEECH Act definitions)

questions.q: Has the person who drafted the GRANITE idea urged Congress to pass the shield and the right to sue as separate bills?
questions.a: This could not be confirmed. In his August 28, 2026 post, Preston Byrne calls H.R. 10174 "a federal sword & shield bill". He also says "Congress would do well to pass it." In a September 8 post, he writes about H.R. 10174 and the HOMEFRONT Act. He says "Each bill would be independently worthy of enactment", meaning each should become law. A plain AI review states that the drafter has urged moving the two parts as separate bills. That statement has not been checked against a source.

s.l: Preston Byrne on H.R. 10174, August 28, 2026
Preston Byrne on the HOMEFRONT Act, H.R. 10309

questions.q: Is there a cost estimate for the GRANITE Act, and who has lobbied on it?
questions.a: No Congressional Budget Office cost estimate for H.R. 10174 was found as of November 12, 2026. The bill has been sent to the House Judiciary Committee and has not been reported out of it. No lobbying disclosure filing naming the bill was identified. Campaign funding of the sponsor and cosponsor in relation to the bill has not been established. Public support has come from Preston Byrne, counsel to 4chan, and from R Street and ITIF (see Stakeholders).

bigger.issue: Foreign rules on online speech that reach Americans and American companies
bigger.lead: The bill works inside American courts. Every court-based law does. Most foreign enforcement happens abroad. It works through foreign offices of companies and foreign internet providers. The tools that reach it are actions by the President, agencies, diplomats and trade officials.

map.part: Enforcing foreign government fines in American courts
map.note: Courts already refuse this under the old rule against enforcing foreign penal laws, meaning laws that punish. The bill writes that rule into law.

map.part: Foreign awards won by private parties under speech laws
map.note: The bill bars them, but it depends on how courts read "law" (another finding in this review).

map.part: Suits by Americans against foreign governments and agencies
map.note: The bill allows a suit for a declaration by a person named in or sent the order. Article III of the Constitution still sets limits on federal courts.

map.part: Penalties for process steps, reports and age checks
map.note: These may fall outside the bill's definition.

map.part: Money damages and legal fees
map.note: The bill does not provide them. Competing proposals add them.

map.part: Federal agency cooperation, court orders for evidence and extradition
map.note: The bill does not address these.

map.part: Orders sent to foreign internet providers, app stores and subsidiaries
map.note: The affected American has no right to sue.

map.part: Fines, blocking and penalties carried out abroad
map.note: No American court can reach these. The executive branch has used visa restrictions, sanctions and trade investigations here. That branch is the President and federal agencies.

map.part: Companies that choose to comply with foreign orders
map.note: The bill does not require anything of companies.

map.part: Foreign libel judgments
map.note: The SPEECH Act already covers these. The bill overlaps with it.

map.part: Tracking how often foreign speech rules reach Americans
map.note: The bill sets no duty to report. The HOMEFRONT Act would require a yearly report from the Attorney General and a list kept by the Federal Trade Commission.

s.l: H.R. 10309, HOMEFRONT Act of 2026, text, Congress.gov

map.part: International evidence and data-sharing agreements
map.note: The bill does not mention the Hague Evidence Convention. The United States has been a party to this treaty since 1972. The bill also does not mention CLOUD Act executive agreements. Those deals already require that a foreign order "may not be used to infringe freedom of speech". Another finding in this review notes this.

s.l: HCCH status table: 1970 Evidence Convention
18 U.S.C. 2523 (CLOUD Act executive agreements)

map.part: Treaties on recognizing foreign judgments
map.note: The United States signed the 2019 Hague Judgments Convention on March 2, 2022. It has not ratified it, which means it has not given final approval. So no treaty on judgments now conflicts with the bar on enforcement.

s.l: HCCH status table: 2019 Judgments Convention
